passages.happening:
‘In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, the month of Chislev’ (verse 1). The people of Bethel had sent men to ask the priests and prophets whether they should still weep and fast in the fifth month, as they had for many years (verses 2-3).

God answers with questions of his own. When they fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for seventy years, was it really for him (verse 5)? And when they ate and drank, was it not for themselves (verse 6)? Were these not the words the earlier prophets proclaimed when Jerusalem was full of people and prosperous (verse 7)?
passages.hearers:
The date is about December 518 BC, nearly two years after the night visions. The temple was half rebuilt.

The fast of the fifth month mourned the burning of the temple by Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, and the fast of the seventh month probably mourned the murder of Gedaliah, the governor left in charge after the fall. Now that the temple was rising, should the mourning stop?

God does not give a yes or no. He asks whether the fasting had ever been about him. Then he points them back to what the prophets before the exile had already said.
passages.later: Second Kings dates the burning of the temple to the fifth month (2 Kings 25:8-9), and tells of Gedaliah's murder in the seventh (2 Kings 25:25). Isaiah described the fast God chooses: ‘to break the chains of wickedness’ (Isaiah 58:6).
passages.hard:
Is God rejecting fasting and religious practice altogether?

No, and the chapter should not be read that way. God does not forbid the fasts, and in 8:19 he promises to turn them into feasts rather than abolishing them. The law itself commanded worship, sacrifice and the fast of the Day of Atonement. What the prophets attack again and again is ritual cut off from justice and mercy, worship that goes on beside oppression. Interpreters in the Jewish and Christian traditions have read this chapter as a call to join outward practice and inward faithfulness rather than to choose between them. Some Protestant readers have stressed the danger of trusting ritual, while Catholic and Orthodox readers have stressed the value of practices rightly kept.
passages.asks: God asks whether the fasting was ever really for him. Ask whom your religious habits are really for. And ask what it would mean to keep them for God rather than for yourself.

passages.t: Justice, mercy, and hearts like flint
passages.happening:
God's word is plain: ‘Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion to one another’ (verse 9). ‘Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor. And do not plot evil in your hearts against one another’ (verse 10).

But the fathers refused to listen. They turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped up their ears (verse 11). ‘They made their hearts like flint’ (verse 12) and would not listen to the law or the words God sent by his Spirit through the prophets, so great anger came. As they would not listen when he called, so he would not listen when they called (verse 13). He scattered them among the nations, and the pleasant land was left desolate (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These verses repeat the message of the prophets before the exile, in brief: true justice in the courts, loyal love and compassion between neighbors, and no oppression of the four groups the law protected, the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner and the poor.

Then they explain why the exile came. It was not that the people lacked rituals. It was that they refused to listen. A stubborn shoulder is the picture of an animal that will not take the yoke. Flint was the hardest stone they knew.

The question from Bethel about fasting is answered with a call to justice. The new community should not repeat its fathers' hardness.
passages.later: The law protected the same four: ‘Do not oppress a foreign resident’ (Exodus 23:9), nor ‘mistreat any widow or orphan’ (Exodus 22:22). Ezekiel promised to take away ‘your heart of stone’ (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.asks: The fathers made their hearts like flint. Ask where your heart has grown hard toward God or toward people. And ask which of the four, the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor, you have been quietest toward.
